caption:
What if you had a trading strategy that never lost a month? 💸🤔

In this classic 60 Minutes clip, we get a rare look at the world of high-frequency trading (HFT) and the simple—yet devastatingly effective—math behind it. The trader explains a basic rule: If a stock drops 5%, buy $5. If it rises 10%, sell $10. Apply this to 4,500 stocks simultaneously using a high-speed computer, and you have a money-making machine that has literally never had a losing month.

📊 The Math of Abundance
This strategy isn't about picking the next Apple or Tesla. It’s about statistical arbitrage. By spreading small bets across thousands of stocks at lightning speed, HFT firms turn the market into a casino where they are the house.

Volume is King: 4,500 stocks at once means the "law of large numbers" works in their favor.

Speed is the Edge: These trades happen in milliseconds, capturing tiny inefficiencies before the retail public even sees the price move.

⚠️ Is the Game Rigged?
Not everyone is a fan. Joe Saluzzi of Themus Trading LLC famously claimed that this high-speed advantage means the "game is rigged" against the average investor. When algorithms can outrun human decision-making by a factor of 1,000, is there still a place for the retail trader?

💡 How to Survive as a Retail Trader in 2026
If the "big boys" are playing a game of speed, your only choice is to play a game of patience. 1. Avoid the Noise: Don't try to out-scalp an algorithm. You will lose every time.
2. Focus on Higher Timeframes: Algorithms dominate the seconds and minutes. Human insight still has an edge in the days, weeks, and months.
3. Use Limit Orders: Never give the HFT machines a free "market order" to nibble on. Control your entry price.

The market has evolved. The floor traders are gone, replaced by servers in data centers humming at the speed of light. But even in a "rigged" game, the disciplined trader who understands the rules can still find a way to win.

caption:
Charlie Munger (January 1, 1924 – November 28, 2023) was an American investor, businessman, attorney, and philanthropist best known as the longtime vice chairman of Berkshire Hathaway. Widely regarded as one of the greatest business thinkers of his generation, Munger played a pivotal role in shaping Berkshire Hathaway alongside Warren Buffett. His multidisciplinary approach to decision-making and emphasis on rational thinking transformed the way countless investors and entrepreneurs approach business and life.

Originally trained as a lawyer, Munger developed an investment philosophy that extended beyond traditional financial analysis. He championed the use of “mental models”—drawing insights from psychology, economics, mathematics, biology, history, and other disciplines—to make better decisions. His influence encouraged investors to focus on acquiring exceptional businesses with durable competitive advantages rather than simply seeking statistically cheap investments.

Known for his sharp wit, intellectual honesty, and straightforward communication, Munger frequently spoke about the importance of patience, lifelong learning, integrity, and avoiding common cognitive biases. His speeches and writings have become foundational resources for investors, business leaders, and decision-makers seeking to improve their judgment and critical thinking.

Munger’s legacy reaches far beyond investing. His philosophy of continuous learning, rationality, and disciplined decision-making has inspired generations of entrepreneurs, executives, and investors around the world. His lifelong partnership with Warren Buffett remains one of the most successful collaborations in business history, demonstrating the lasting value of clear thinking, sound judgment, and unwavering principles.

Topics: Mental Models • Rational Thinking • Value Investing • Decision-Making • Lifelong Learning

#CharlieMunger #ValueInvesting #BerkshireHathaway #DecisionMaking #LifelongLearning
transcript: Are there any tools or behaviors you embrace to facilitate your rational thinking? The answer is of course, how do they do anything else? One of my favorite tricks is the inversion process. I'll give you an example, when I was a meteorologist in World War, they told me how to draw weather maps and predict the weather, but what I was actually doing is clearing pilots to take flights. It just reversed the problem, I inverted it. I said suppose I wanted to kill a lot of pilots, what would be the easy way to do it? I soon concluded the only easy way to do it would be to get the planes into icing the planes couldn't handle, or to get the pilot to a place where he'd run out of fuel before he could safely land. So I made up my mind I was going to stay miles away from killing pilots by either icing or getting them into sock conditions when they couldn't land. I think that helped me be a better meteorologist in World War. I just reversed the problem. If somebody hired me to fix India, I would immediately say, what could I do if I really wanted to hurt India? I'd figure out all the things that would most easily hurt India, and I'd figure out how to avoid them. You'd say it's the same thing, it's just in reverse. It works better to free them to invert the problem. You're a meteorologist, it really helps if you really know how to avoid something, which is the only thing that's going to kill your pilot. You can help India best if you understand what will really hurt India the easiest and worst. Algebra works the same way. Every great algebraist inverts all the time, because the problems are solved easier. Human beings should do the same thing in the ordinary walks of life. It's constantly a burden. You don't think of what you want, you think what you want to avoid. But when you're thinking what you want to avoid, you also think about what you want. You just go back and forth all the time.

caption:
The CNBC fight that cracked Wall Street on live TV.
On March 31, 2014, Brad Katsuyama went on CNBC and publicly accused the market of being rigged — sitting feet away from William O’Brien, a senior executive at BATS Global Markets.
The backdrop wasn’t drama — it was data.
At the time, high-frequency firms were responsible for 50–60% of all U.S. equity trading volume, using speed advantages measured in microseconds to detect and trade ahead of slower orders.
Katsuyama claimed exchanges were selling:
• Proprietary data feeds
• Co-location (servers inside exchange data centers)
• Complex order types
...creating a two-tier market:
